text:
What it is: A register books fixed recurring meetings for paired units, and a leaver vouches in the newcomer.

How it works: A housing authority or co-op pairs each opted-in unit with two others, favoring renter-owner mixes. Pairs meet 45 minutes every other week at a fixed time in a neutral ground-floor room, reminded 48 hours ahead; three-month terms end in renewal or blameless release, and notice to vacate triggers a handover. A pilot randomizes units, tracking attendance and loneliness.

text:
What it is: A program for new movers.

How it works: Registering an address triggers an invitation to a cohort of six to ten arrivals within a ten-minute walk. Arrival leave covers eight days of three-hour hosted meals with staged mutual disclosure, then sessions on days 10, 13, 17, 22, 30, 40, 55; a gap widens only if a weekly one-tap check shows self-made meetups. No mixers run meanwhile; contact details unlock after shared attendance; a separate custodian holds attendance-only records.

text:
What it is: It ties a resident's recurring purchases to one staff member at a fixed slot, so repeat contact becomes recognition.

How it works: Both sides opt in; residents name 3-5 weekly errands: café, pharmacy, grocery pickup, parcel desk. A scheduler matches each to a recurring shift slot, the app nudges visit time, and visits open with a fixed two-line exchange and one rotating prompt. New addresses trigger re-pinning nearby, and a public subsidy pays employers per continuity hour.

text:
What it is: Paid residents acknowledge whoever enters a marked ward, so being noticed costs no one spare time.

How it works: Wards are lit, glass-walled, sound-damped transit-hub bays; crossing the floor line requests acknowledgment, and stepping out ends approaches. Two paid witnesses per two-hour shift, phones away, nod at entrants, learn opt-in names, introduce regulars to successors, and send an opt-in note after two missed visits. Logged shifts mint an unlinkable, revocable credential; a ring tap lights green; newcomers get three welcome visits.

text:
What it is: An opt-in scheme that repeatedly seats the same verified people together at shared tables where waiting is compulsory, turns their time together into recorded shared hours, and later uses those records to seat them with their partners' partners.

How it works: Commuter coaches, laundromats, clinics and sport sidelines reserve tables of four to six seats at fixed slots, and an assigner reseats you with the same people each time. To sit, two verified IDs tap a fixed post within two seconds, and each person sees the other's name, district and shared partners only once both commit. Posts log co-present minutes; after forty hours a pair can tap to mint one co-signed, undeletable record of total hours. Arriving elsewhere, you are seated with holders of a shared partner, ranked by the weaker record.

text:
What it is: A scheme housing mutually named tenants close together when either moves, so invested hours keep accruing instead of resetting.

How it works: Social, co-op and large-landlord networks keep a registry where two tenants name each other, at most two each, renewed six-monthly, silent opt-out. When one moves, a unit is offered in the other's stairwell or block, or adjacent if both move, fees waived. Vacancies are batched quarterly so arrivals share a floor and move-in week.

text:
What it is: A relay offers outings only to neighbours with high private lean, plus a paid district hour.

How it works: Blocks of about 40 verified households hold a private lean that rises with taps and decays unseen. A resident heading to the courtyard table taps "there till 20:40", and the relay sends one unrepeated message only to neighbours above their learned threshold, if two qualify. Newcomers start at a settled neighbour's lean; every third Thursday a city-paid 90-minute early release by postcode resets everyone.

text:
What it is: An opt-in lease program testing newcomer ties.

How it works: The building sends newcomer parcel, key, or tool requests to two adjacent households; answers within 24 hours carry the tie. After two misses, a two-person crew logs each side's barrier (safety, language, shifts, grievance), applies a remedy (ID check, interpreter, slot choice, mediation), runs an eight-minute task, then seven seated minutes without phones, leaving first. Re-test after seven days, up to four times, then re-match; redo after upheaval.

text:
What it is: A system in which people who regularly use the same transit stops can verify one another through records of their tap-ins, so that approaching a stranger feels safe, and can then arrange to meet at graded levels of contact.

How it works: Posts at busy stops log taps from ID-verified NFC tokens, and someone is resolved to you after 15 or more tap days over 45 or more days. If they appear only when you do, or their arrival shifts when yours does, they are flagged as aligned. To meet, you tap Open and pick a grade: nod, name, or walk to the platform. Mutually resolved Open pairs are sent to numbered pavement marks, where both see the lower grade and their shared stop history, and identity is escrowed and released only on complaint.

text:
What it is: A way to keep new resident ties warm by removing cold contacts.

How it works: A 21-day window opens at move-in booking: a paid steward does the newcomer's chores; four verified residents each host one potluck-equal turn in a lobby room. On day 21, pairs privately opt in; mutual matches are shielded. Disputes go anonymously via the steward, with no shared committees or chores, a nod discharges obligation, and the only prompt is a one-ping "open" flag.

text:
What it is: A lease requirement ties each apartment unit to three to five other units through small, reciprocal chores, and the arrangement passes to the next tenant at move-out, so a newcomer's first contact with neighbors is a task they owe.

How it works: Each lease lists the bonded units and a chore menu of catching parcels, holding a spare key, watering plants, and heatwave check-ins, while a ledger app routes requests so favors balance both ways. Optional personal ties last 13 weeks and renew in a quarterly building-wide window by double-blind mutual opt-in, so an ending reveals no rejection. At move-out a mediator privately polls bonded units and resets any flagged bond, and the leaver walks the newcomer to each bonded door.

text:
What it is: Laundromats and building laundry rooms would offer a discounted long, low-heat cycle booked as a standing weekly berth for seven residents who live within walking distance, in 13-week terms starting on lease-quarter boundaries.

How it works: In weeks 1 to 4 the seats face the machines and silence is fine, and at week 4 each member privately opts in or moves berth. In weeks 5 to 9 members share a table of rooting cuttings, and in weeks 10 to 13 the seats face each other. In the last session, each member braids one strand into a cord.

text:
What it is: A group of six to eight households on one stair shares a wooden baton that is passed from door to door in a fixed order.

How it works: The baton has a mechanical tally and comes with a route card listing door numbers only. The holder clicks the tally and hangs the baton on the next listed handle within 24 hours. Each full circuit, about one week, adds to the ring count. If the baton is 48 hours late, the downstream door knocks upstream, while a hold tag skips a household without a knock. When someone leaves, the doors beside them are rewritten as adjacent, newcomers receive the baton within days and are inserted, and each season one adjacent pair swaps.

text:
What it is: Residents who opt in get an e-paper door plate showing a 16x16 glyph they drew, which fades each day unless other residents tap it with their fob.

How it works: The plate's contrast depends on how many distinct residents tapped it in the last 7 days, from gray at none to full at three or more. Each resident can tap a given plate once a day, not their own, and the tapper's glyph shows in the corner until midnight. There are no names, counts or cloud logs, and quiet mode shows contrast only. New plates start full with a border for 14 days.

text:
What it is: A way for two people to find out how willing each is to interact, by comparing punched cards so that only the lower level is revealed, and that lower level limits what they do next.

How it works: Laundromats and clinic waiting rooms give each pair with overlapping waits a card split by a random notched cut, and taking a half is optional. Each person privately punches zero to three holes from the left, meaning nod, chat while waiting, or swap contacts. Later, either may ask to read the card, and both slide halves into a lightbox from opposite sides, where only matching notches seat. The lit holes show the lower level, no light means the card was not taken, and fresh cards are re-punched, so levels can fall.

text:
What it is: Two thumb-held tokens co-sign rate-capped increments, logged within 24 hours, so rind width reflects years of shared hours that any stranger can verify by tap.

How it works: Libraries issue one token per person, in person. A seam grows only while tokens stay within 1.5 m by UWB and owners re-thumb every 20 minutes. Credit caps at one hour per pair daily, first ten hours only in certified public seats. Each increment carries a drand value and blinded entry.

text:
What it is: A glass basin that residents fill by fob taps to unlock a courtyard slot.

How it works: Each tap adds one cup, one per person, at the lobby too; a bell siphon empties only at N cups. A flow switch lights and heats the courtyard and texts pledgers the next 45-minute slot. A chime rings faster past 70% full, cups drain in 24 hours, basins hold 4, 8 or 16 cups, firings lock adjacent basins, and arrivals get 3 cups.

text:
What it is: A plan to retrofit a block of about 12 to 40 flats with a fifth-generation ambient loop, so that each flat's heat pump shares one pipe and neighbours' waste heat warms it and lowers bills.

How it works: Each heat pump draws from and dumps into the shared pipe, which anchors such as bakery ovens, shop chillers and a laundrette feed first. Billing is per tap with the operator only, never shared between neighbours, and a wall strip glows with the share of heat from the loop, pooled over at least three flats. With consent, a flat silent on the loop for 36 hours gets an automatic ping and then a knock from a paid steward, and detaching takes one valve and a form.

text:
What it is: A city scheme where paired residents tap posts kilometres apart within 60 seconds, with pay rising as separation grows.

How it works: Residents enrol, pick a post and slot, and are paired with someone 3+ km away. In a 60-second voice or text channel both tap and rate an item such as odour, noise or haze, earning transit credit scaled by distance. Large disagreement triggers a third-post re-sampling, either may skip, and a move re-scores the pair.

text:
What it is: A ground-floor, street-facing community kitchen for about 300 homes, where commercial equipment and wholesale food reduce the cost and time of meals, but only while three badge holders staff three stations at once.

How it works: The stations are Prep with blades, Cook with a combi oven, and Pack, which is seated for portioning, sealing, and logging temperatures. An app lists open stations in 90-minute blocks, with one Pack slot held for arrivals, and new groups of three cook set recipes and each take about nine portions at wholesale cost. The log counts co-runs per pair, and six unlock own recipes, cooking for kids, and standing swaps.
